Camp Horizon · sample exchange

The pawn shop

The mission left Earth with $1.0B and 1,000 MWh. The ship spent most of the cash; the flight burned most of the power. Sell what you dig, drill and drive back for cash, earn power by running the camp and the rover — and buy your ride home.

Half the size, a third of the pull

Living on Mars time is strange: every sol is about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day, so a Mars clock slowly drifts away from Earth's. Mission teams for the Mars rovers have lived on "Mars time", shifting their sleep later every day.

02 · Orbit

Where Mars is right now

Mars's orbit is stretched, so its distance from the Sun swings between 207 and 249 million km. Earth catches up with Mars about every 26 months. Spacecraft launch just before that, on a curved transfer orbit that meets Mars about 8 months later.

Earth–Mars distance · drag to travel in time · ▲ launch window
Earth to Mars—Straight-line distance
Radio delay—One way, at light speed
Season on Mars—Northern hemisphere
Next close approach—Earth between Sun and Mars
Next launch window—Ideal Hohmann launch date
Trip on that orbit≈ 259 daysAbout 8½ months
↻

Seasons of different lengths

Mars tilts 25.2°, so it has seasons. Because the orbit is stretched, northern spring lasts 194 sols but northern autumn only 142. Southern summer comes when Mars is closest to the Sun, so it's warmer and it's the main dust-storm season.

Positions from NASA JPL's approximate orbital elements. They reproduce the 2018 to 2025 close approaches to within a day. Real missions launch within a few weeks of the ideal date.

03 · Interior

Listening to marsquakes

NASA's InSight lander recorded 1,319 marsquakes from 2018 to 2022. Seismic waves bounced off the planet's core and back to InSight, revealing what lies inside. Here Mars is sliced open along the path from the quake to InSight. Drag to turn the planet, and click anywhere on its surface to set off a new marsquake.

Distance to quake——
Direct S wave—Straight through the mantle
Core echo (ScS)—Bounced off the core

InSight's position is real, and most of its quakes came from Cerberus Fossae, about 1,700 km away. The other places are what-if quakes. Wave speed simplified to 4.5 km/s and paths drawn straight. Crust drawn thicker than scale.

Crust 24–72 km thick

The rocky outer shell, thicker in the southern highlands than in the northern plains. Patches of it are magnetized: fossils of a global magnetic field Mars lost billions of years ago.

Mantle to ~1,600 km deep

Hot silicate rock. Its cold, rigid top layer is several hundred kilometres thick, which is why Mars has no moving tectonic plates. That is how volcanoes like Olympus Mons grew so tall: they stayed over the same hot spot.

Liquid core radius ~1,650–1,850 km

Molten iron with lots of sulfur and other light elements. It is surprisingly large and light, about half the planet's radius. Without a churning solid–liquid core like Earth's, Mars has no global magnetic shield today.

Biggest marsquake 4 May 2022

InSight's largest quake was magnitude 4.7. Its waves circled the planet, and its echoes helped measure the core.

02 · Atmosphere

Why there are no lakes today

The air is so thin that a cup of water would boil and freeze at the same time — try it.

❄

The air freezes

In winter so much carbon dioxide freezes onto the pole that air pressure across Mars drops by about a quarter, then rises again in spring.

◐

Blue sunsets

By day the dusty sky is butterscotch. At sunset, fine dust scatters red light away and lets blue light through around the Sun.

03 · Water

Where did the water go?

Mars once had rivers and lakes; most of that water escaped to space and the rest is frozen underground — which is where you'll drill for it.

For comparison

Mars figures from NASA Goddard (Villanueva et al. 2015). Mars lost most of its early water to space.

Polar ice caps

The ice at the south pole alone could cover the whole planet about 11 metres deep.

Ground ice

Across the high latitudes, ice sits centimetres to metres under the soil. Phoenix touched it in 2008.

Ancient rivers and lakes

Dry deltas, channels and clay minerals record a time when liquid water flowed.

Why it matters for survival

Water is the most valuable thing on Mars. You can drink it, grow food with it, split it into oxygen to breathe, and turn it into rocket fuel for the trip home.

06 · Moons

Two moons that break the rules

Phobos orbits faster than Mars spins, so it rises in the west and sets in the east, twice a sol. Deimos orbits a little slower than Mars spins and creeps from east to west over about two and a half sols. Stand on the Martian equator and watch.

"Fear" · the inner moon

Fate: falling inIt orbits inside the dashed ring, so tides drag it about 1.8 m closer every century. In 30 to 50 million years it will crash into Mars or break up into a ring.

Its biggest crater, Stickney, is about 9 km wide, almost half the moon. The impact nearly shattered it.

Orbits to scale · time-lapse
A spot on Mars's equator, carried round once a sol
Areostationary orbit, 20,428 km from the centre: one lap takes exactly one sol
Inside it, a moon laps the surface and spirals in. Outside, it lags behind and drifts out.

Deimos

"Dread" · the outer moon
Average width12.4 km
Distance from Mars's centre23,460 km
One orbit30 h 18 min
Seen from the surfaceA bright star
Fate: drifting awayIt orbits outside the dashed ring, so it is very slowly moving outward, like our own Moon.

Both moons were found by Asaph Hall in 1877. JAXA's MMX mission plans to bring a piece of Phobos to Earth to learn whether they are captured asteroids or debris from a giant impact.

01 · Design, then launch

Build it, lift it, fly it

First the Assembly Bay: pick a launch vehicle and fit instruments, power, radios and cargo into the ship like blocks. More science means more mass, more power and more data to send home — and your budget is $900M. Then the pad: thirty seconds of debris between you and Mars orbit.

No launches yet

Launch Centre

The rocket game opens full-screen. Steer with ← → or A / D, drag on touch, or use the on-screen buttons. Thirty seconds, three hull points, as many rocks as space can throw. There is no retry button: every flight ends in a report card, and only a flight that reaches Mars orbit unlocks the Mars world.

Trade-offsA core drill is top science, but 40 kg and 150 W. A camera is 4 kg — and 150 Mbit of pictures a sol to radio home.
Max-QA minute after lift-off the air pushes hardest on the rocket. Real rockets throttle down for it.
Orbit, then MarsAt 7.8 km/s you're in orbit. Burn to 11.4 km/s and Earth lets go of you.
ShieldsBlue shields block one hit. Spacecraft carry real "Whipple" shields for exactly this.
No brakesNothing slows you down out here. The only way to miss a rock is to not be where it is.
02 · The gap

How far is Mars, really?

Far enough that light takes up to 22 minutes. Far enough that no one on Earth can steer for you.

56 million kmClosest Earth and Mars ever get. It happens once every 26 months — that's why launch windows exist.
401 million kmFarthest apart, when the Sun is in the way and radio goes quiet for weeks.
259 daysThe cheapest route — half an ellipse around the Sun. Faster costs far more fuel.
1.8 mSv a dayRadiation in deep space, measured by the Curiosity rover on its way out. About a chest X-ray every day.

Mission design · Step 2 of 3 · trade study

Plan the flight

Three choices: when to launch, how fast to go, how to arrive. Faster costs energy and payload; slower costs crew health. This is the trade study NASA's Mission Design Lab runs before a point design; the energy and Δv come from the first-cut method a GMAT user starts with.
